en: I. Discourse on Encouraging Merit:
Having attained human birth through hundreds of hardships, and having secured this rare opportunity so difficult to find, while death—inescapable and most cruel—stands perpetually before you;
Those who have not prepared in abundance the provisions for the journey consisting of self-restraint, generosity, and discipline,
will encounter sufferings when they have fallen into the steep precipices of the fierce ocean of saṃsāra.
Having attained this human birth, which is difficult to find and as flickering as a flash of lightning,
one should direct the mind either toward the destruction of existence or toward the requisites for worldly existence.
Having attained human birth, which is as flickering as a wave of lightning’s flame, one should perform only meritorious deeds here; for this is the wish-fulfilling gem for men.
By whose power you have now once again attained this human state,
let that merit increase here, for it is the cause of your happiness.
That human birth which you have obtained by relying upon merit, and which is now endowed with various qualities such as nobility of form, high lineage, and so forth—
that merit alone is your friend and the sole kinsman of all beings in other lives.
Therefore, perform this repeatedly; it brings about the attainment of all goals.

By relying upon those very merits, you have attained sovereignty esteemed by the world, which is the abode of Fortune; therefore, you should cause those merits to increase further, for one must never diminish the side of those who have been beneficial.
Desist from evil; perform most noble merit;
subdue the difficult-to-tame horse of the mind that craves sense objects;
and, like the lords of sages, be constantly devoted to the welfare of others.
As long as the serpent of death has not yet bitten with its unbearable venom.
Thus concludes the discourse on the encouragement of merit.
II. Discourse on Encouraging the Hearing of the Dharma:

Having understood this wondrous and fleeting opportunity—which is as difficult to encounter as the meeting of the opening of a tortoise's neck with the hole of a yoke floating upon the ocean—[one should listen to the Dharma].
Listen for even a moment to the word of the Sage, which is exceedingly difficult to encounter in this world, the sole path to the city of peace, and the remover of the fear of calamity.

That human birth, free from the defects of the eight inopportune states, which is difficult to obtain even in many hundreds of aeons, has now been attained; therefore, you must indeed exert yourselves to hear the Dharma.
In this worldly existence, which is as flickering as a drop of water on the tip of a young leaf and is enveloped by the web of afflictions,
the birth of one who does not contemplate the true path of action is fruitless in this world.

Not by those gone to hell, nor by hungry ghosts, nor by those in the animal realm, nor by those with impaired faculties, nor by those who honor the gods, nor by those dwelling in border regions, nor by those wounded by the sword of false views;
for the Sun-like Sage, the Victor, has not yet risen with the light of wisdom.
The nectar of the words of the Lord of Sages can be drunk by both humans and gods.

Therefore, having abandoned all unwholesome actions and recognizing one's own duty to be the supreme noble Dharma, the Dharma should indeed be listened to with diligence; for from it, all virtues arise.
This jewel of speech from the Lord of Sages first brings joy to the wise at the very moment it falls upon the ear; thereafter, it destroys the mass of powerful, heavy, and dense darkness;
and finally, at the conclusion of reflection and meditation, it makes manifest the entire continuity of the cycle of birth.
It constantly shatters the entire series of afflictions and is the treasury of all prosperity.
It removes the calamities arising from intense existence and bestows the unsurpassed bliss of nirvāṇa;
having thus understood these words of the Sage, listen now with pure minds.
Thus ends the discourse on the encouragement to listen to the Dharma.

III. Discourse on the Rarity of Human Birth: Having obtained that which enables one to cross even the ocean of existence and to plant the seed of supreme enlightenment leading to auspiciousness—human birth, which exceeds even the wish-fulfilling gem in its abundance of virtues—who here would render it fruitless? (SRKK 15)
That person who, having obtained a human birth through numerous eons of virtuous resources, fails out of delusion to accumulate even the slightest wealth of merit in this world,
encounters intense sorrow upon departing from this life to the next.
Like a merchant who has returned from an island of jewels empty-handed to his own home.
Human birth is not obtained again through unwholesome paths of action;
when human birth is not obtained, there is only suffering—where, then, is happiness?
There is no greater deception than this, nor any greater delusion,
than to fail to perform much wholesome merit upon encountering such a moment as this.
For a sin committed in a single moment, one dwells in Avīci for an eon;
how much more so for a sin committed over many lifetimes—what need is there to speak of a happy rebirth?
For this very reason, the Blessed One said: "Human birth is exceedingly difficult to obtain, comparable to a turtle inserting its neck through the hole of a yoke in the great ocean. (SRKK 20)
Thus ends the discourse on the rarity of human birth.
IV. Discourse on Giving:
An abundance of food, drink, beds, and seats; jewels, garlands, garments, and ornaments;
fame, supreme virtues, and young women—all this is said to come from giving. (SRKK 21)

From giving, one obtains the radiance of authority, the excellence of enjoyments, preeminent beauty and magnanimity, sweetness of complexion, vigor, eloquence of speech, luster, health, and long life; such is the desired fruit of each respective gift.

Horses, silken garments, elephants, fly-whisks white with many flowers, parasols, palaces filled with music, the sounds of honeyed drums, flower garlands, young women, food, jewels, necklaces, cities, towns, the earth, saffron, and the world of the gods.
And the state of perfect buddhahood is declared by the Buddhas here to be the fruit of the wish-fulfilling tree of giving.
And those women, whose eyes rival the delicate and stainless petals of the blue lotus, whose thighs and hips are kissed by shimmering girdles, whose red garments have slipped away,
and whose creeper-like brows are arched as their breasts heave— these very women now enter into servitude.
This is the manifestation of generosity, which is skillful in shattering the door-panel of stinginess.
Those best of men who always travel with horses whose heads are bowed under the weight of chowries, with elephants whose mouths are turned upward by their bits and whose rut has been broken,
and who are constantly honored by servants adorned with ornaments and joined palms; [they too must eventually depart].
The sages declare that such is the fruit of giving from what was previously acquired.
Adorned with necklaces, gold bracelets inlaid with diamonds,
armlets, and crowns studded with jewels, these kings always sit upon lion-thrones and sport with various diversions in the midst of their harem women.
The sages declare that to be the fruit of giving, known as the Śārdūlavikrīḍita.

In a palace inlaid with jewels, gems, and gold, adorned with parasols and banners, resounding with the songs of lutes, flutes, and harps, and illuminated by the radiance of precious stones— where Śakra, accompanied by Śacī and surrounded by thousands of women, takes his delight.
The sages declare that such is the fruit of giving from what was previously acquired.
The giver constantly attains the affection of people and is attended by many virtuous persons who approach him;
his stainless fame spreads in all directions, and being confident, he attains that very state.

Upon the dissolution of the body, having attained rebirth among the gods in places where various abundant and radiant enjoyments are found, he dwells for a very long time without weariness, experiencing supreme happiness at will in gardens such as Nandana, which abound with vast wish-fulfilling trees covered in blossoming clusters of diverse flowers.
Through its offering, one attains [a state] served by celestial maidens of most excellent form.

Generosity is indeed a great treasure that follows one [into the next life] and cannot be shared with thieves or others; it is the washing away of the dust of the faults of stinginess and greed from the mind,
and generosity is a comfortable vehicle that removes the exhaustion of the path of saṃsāra.
Generosity is a true friend that provides manifold comforts and is eternal.
With girdles fastened at their hips, voices sweet as warbling, brows moving gracefully in play,
large and lovely eyes reaching to their ears, and garlands resting upon the ends of their hair—
these women themselves come into the service of the virtuous, their broad hips full and firm.
The son of Śuddhodana spoke of that greatness of giving, which brings about its gathered fruit.

The lover repeatedly drinks the honey, as red as the *bandhūka* flower, which has been poured into a beautiful golden vessel; it is fragrant with crushed mango blossoms, contains swaying submerged lotuses, and was offered by his beloved as a solemn oath.
Those of pure intellect declare that therein, giving is the supreme cause for the highest good.
Having thus heard these virtues of giving, O gentle one, apply yourself with a disciplined mind to the practice of generosity;
for in this world of the three realms, amidst its fierce and great terrors, there is no other kinsman for humanity superior to giving.
Thus concludes the discourse on generosity.
V. Discourse on Merit:

Whatever is most beautiful or dear seen in the world—be it form, lineage, loved ones, wealth, or happiness—the virtuous declare that these are created solely by the artisan of merit; they are not equal to the merit of a person who performs wholesome deeds.
Adorned with rows of exceedingly tall, lofty, and white banners, and accompanied by vast multitudes of troops agitated by elephants, horses, infantry, and chariots,
kings of great merit move upon the earth, their physical splendor graced by waving chowries.

That certain men alone bear such splendor— clothed in garments of silk, Kāśika cotton, and fine linen, their limbs adorned with strings of pearls and ornaments of gold and jewels— is the gratitude for their own past deeds of merit.
A very long life, birth in a noble family, a beautiful body, freedom from the fear of disease,
abundant wealth, and the excellence of a retinue— these are the great fruits of merit.
That a universal monarch, though endowed with the most excellent jewels and a thousand sons, enjoyed the earth bounded by the ocean— that is the vast fruit of the jewel of merit.

Seated in the midst of a variegated lotus posture, always saluted by the lords of gods and asuras, Brahmā always shines with such splendor that he outshines even the world of Brahmā; this is indeed due to his merit.
That the Teacher of Gods is always worshipped by the hosts of gods, nāgas, asuras, and siddhas, as well as by gandharvas, yakṣas, and supreme kinnaras— that is the vast fruit of the jewel of merit.
Leaving behind their physical form, vigor, and craft, men depart helplessly from this world to the next, driven by the winds of karma.
But merit alone follows one here absolutely and brings about happiness;
because it cannot be taken away by others, merit is the most excellent of all riches.
Even those winds of universal dissolution, which by their force scatter even Mount Meru in the ten directions, are not capable of destroying merit.
Merit does not undergo corruption by the waters of the four oceans, which surge forth unrestrained during the dissolution of the world.
Even when the earth is being consumed by the seven sun-fires, which are like blazing coals of light, a single act of merit is not burned away.
Thus concludes the discourse on merit.
VI. The Story of Bimba:

He was wealthy, with sorrow destroyed, all strife eliminated, a vessel for the joy of the eyes, a treasury of the splendor of good fortune, his body possessed of well-developed strength, and renowned for his glory.
Having fashioned an image of the Blessed Buddha, one becomes radiant, beautiful in form, eloquent in speech, with all the horses of the senses subdued, manifest, wise, and a generous giver. (SRKK 46)
As many atoms as there are in the stupas or images of the Blessed One, so many kingdoms shall the maker of them certainly enjoy in heaven and on earth;
and having experienced all the bliss of the perfection of the meditative absorptions of the form and formless realms, he shall enjoy it all.
Before long, one attains the state of a Buddha, which is free from birth, old age, and misfortune.

One who fashions an image of the Tathāgata shall become a Victor at the end, having conquered the enemies that are the faults— a universal monarch endowed with the thirty-two marks of excellence and adorned with beautiful limbs.
The non-deficiency of the sense faculties, being far removed from womanhood and the miserable realms,
birth as a human, a noble lineage, and speech that is accepted as authoritative.
Birth, sacred learning, tradition, fortitude, the attainment of desired goals, steadfastness in appropriate matters, and freedom from the affliction of passion and other such defilements; SRKK_50 //
By fashioning an image of the Buddha or a stūpa for living beings at all times, there arise distinctions esteemed by the virtuous known as "perfect awakening."

He who fashions an image of the Lord of the World does not fall into servitude, nor into a state of poverty, nor into being a messenger, nor even into a low birth; nor shall he suffer any deficiency of the sense faculties in this world.
Thus ends the story of the image.
VII. Discourse on Bathing:
Whoever bathes the Sugata with various fragrant perfumes, or performs worship with flowers, incense, and unguents, or with sounds of musical instruments played with a joyful mind;
At the end, he bathes in the Mandākinī, which is pervaded by the pollen of the filaments of blossoming golden lotuses; cleansed of all sins and impurities, he attains liberation.
In the Mandākinī, which is agitated by the heavy blows from the full and lofty breasts and hips of celestial women,
and which casts about the fragrance of the overflowing sweet nectar falling from blossoming golden lotuses,
the hosts of gods daily take delight in water-sports.
This is the fruit of bathing the venerable Buddha with various kinds of scented water.

Whatever person performs this bathing of the Sage with musk, sandalwood, camphor, saffron, and excellent fragrant substances— possessing a delightful scent and a luster that is dark, white, red, and yellow— [attains the highest merit].
He becomes one whose mind is free from stain; so say those who are themselves stainless.
Thus ends the discourse on bathing.

VIII. The Story of Saffron and Other Fragrances: When the Lord of the Gods bathes in the Mandākinī, its broad and blossoming lotuses are spread apart by the hands, breasts, hips, and thighs of the playful women at the bathing ghats.

The fruit [obtained] from repeatedly offering fragrant water for the feet, incense, flowers, garlands, and perfumes out of reverence to the Supreme Being by beloved women overwhelmed by passion— [that fruit is attained].

When the universal monarch, experiencing supreme physical bliss in the Ganges— which is joined with streams of saffron water carried through the sky by clouds, fragrant with the scent of camphor and cooled by contact with the fragrance of Malaya sandalwood— rejoices together with beautiful women.
Therefore, by the renunciation of saffron and other such things, [one should offer] to the venerable Buddha, who is a treasury of the jewels of virtue.
By making offerings of mṛdaṅgas, vīṇās, and paṭahas to the most excellent Sugatas,
one hears the sounds of gods and humans and attains a distinguished, divine ear.
Thus ends the account of the saffron and other [substances].
IX. The Discourse on the Parasol:
That universal monarch (cakravartin) travels through the sky with an umbrella, accompanied by elephants, horses, infantry, and chariots, the seven jewels, and a thousand sons.
Even that fruit which obstructs the rays of the sun with a parasol having the halo of the moon as its cover was produced from the gift of a parasol.

Whoever offers to a shrine a parasol adorned with a multitude of various colored, fragrant flowers, their mass swaying from the feet of hovering bees that hum with song, and beautified by an array of many-colored blossoms, together with beautiful and variegated ribbons; [for him, there shall be a parasol of sovereignty].
For he certainly attains the lordship over the four continents, which is honored by the rulers of the earth.

With the rays of the sun obscured by their golden parasols, seated upon the shoulders of majestic, well-trained elephants, adorned with excellent ornaments of many jewels, and rivaling the splendor of Śakra,
the sovereigns who rule over the four continents travel through the sky with ease.
That is the fruit resulting from the offering of flowers and parasols at a stūpa containing the relic of a Tathāgata.
Thus ends the story of the parasol.
X. Discourse on the Entrustment of the Elements:

One who is immediately well-established in the words of the perfections of the Sugata becomes one whose fame is proclaimed upon the earth and who serves as the refuge for the entire realm of sentient beings.
If the relics are enshrined by people within an image of the Victor, provided it possesses a foundation of an exceedingly lofty and stable nature, [the merit is immeasurable].
Having attained sovereign splendor on all sides and enjoyed the four continents as lords of men,
kings at the end attain the pure state through the transference into the realm of the Victor.
Those mortals seen in the world of men who are radiant, with faces like the moon, beautiful brows, and long eyes; those who resemble excellent gold and are endowed with patience and gentleness;
and that universal monarch who protects the earth girt by the oceans—[all these are seen because of patience].
All that becomes [manifest] in the image of the Buddha for embodied beings who, through devotion, have projected the element [of their consciousness] upon it.
Thus concludes the discourse on the conferral of the elements.

XI. One who constructs this maṇḍala in the abode of the Sugata, the supreme one, will be golden-hued, liberated from all diseases, distinguished among gods and men, and radiant with splendor like the moon; he will be enriched with wealth and gold and be born into a royal lineage. (SRKK 65)

Those who create mandalas with flowers for the Buddha, who is honored by the three worlds, suddenly attain sovereignty over people; they become long-lived and are liberated from the fears of various diseases. (SRKK 66)
Generosity is cow dung mixed with water; ethical discipline is sweeping; patience is the removal of small ants; vigor is the exertion of activity;
meditation is making the mind one-pointed for that moment; and wisdom is the bright, well-drawn lines.
Having constructed the mandala of the Sage, one obtains these very six perfections.
Endowed with divine pleasures and all the finest enjoyments, mortals become possessed of a most beautiful complexion surpassing gold;
with lotus-like faces, flawless limbs, and wide eyes, they adorn the earth with various flowers of the Gaṇas.
Thus concludes the discourse on the maṇḍala.
XII. Discourse on Food:

In the city of the gods, that which was held by the lotus-like hands of beloved women—resplendent with excellent color and fragrance, and pleasant to the taste and touch—was enjoyed by the hosts of deities and the most eminent gods.
They consume divine nectar placed in vessels of radiant gold;
this is the fruit of giving food offered toward the Noble Saṅgha headed by the Buddha.

Having conquered the enemy of Smara along with his servants through loving-kindness upon the adamantine seat, and having likewise brought under control the enemies that are the afflictions, the internal objects of the senses, the wicked ones who move within,
as well as the enemy that is the aggregates and death itself by force, the Sugata—
He too has attained mastery over the enjoyment of the finest of all flavors through the power of giving food.

Through the gift of food, the wise person attains a life span, strength, complexion, and noble form, endowed with all limbs complete and possessed of glorious happiness and peerless eloquence. (SRKK 71)

Those lords of men who, having conquered enemies endowed with strength and valor and having attained prosperity, enjoy delicious foods—it is indeed always due to their previous giving of food that this occurs. (SRKK 72)
Thus ends the discourse on eating.
XIII. Discourse on Drinks:
That stainless honey, red as a ruby, placed within a golden vessel, mixed with snow, and resting in the center of a swaying blue lotus—how desirable it is!
That which is offered by one's beloved with eyes slightly reddened and accompanied by the sound of music is drunk by the best of men; such is the fruit resulting from the gift of drink.
Indeed, in vessels made of gold and inlaid with the finest gems such as lapis lazuli and sapphire,
the gods, together with divine women whose chests are covered by the weight of their jar-like breasts,
drink sweet honey-wine or *mādhava* liquor, absorbed in the joy of drinking.
The wise have declared that the delightful fruit of giving a drink to a multitude gathered for a festival is [as great as] that very same fruit.
That drink which is endowed with qualities such as color and fragrance, prepared to destroy thirst and expert at pacifying phlegm, humors, and severe wind— this powder of *pippalī* fragments,
refined in summer within a vessel resembling moonbeams and cooled by snow; that [is it].
Having given [it] with devotion to the Saṅgha, one who has gone to the celestial abode of the gods obtains divine drink.
He who respectfully offers a drink as sweet as honey and sublime to an excellent assembly shall,
for a long time, drink the foremost of beverages, presented by exquisite women, both in heaven and throughout the entire world.
Those people on earth who, with minds clear through faith, offer excellent drinks to the Saṅgha at the proper time,
dwell upon the slopes of the mountain caves of saṃsāra and constantly obtain sweet, fine drinks.
Thus ends the discourse on drink.

XIV. Those who offer to the Teacher of the World, together with his supreme retinue, garlands of radiant garments fashioned from various colors— blue, yellow, green, crimson, white, and variegated— shall obtain their desired and most excellent robes.
He who, with faith and devotion, offers a robe and a garland to the Saṅgha, the most excellent among all assemblies,
shall obtain the garment of modesty— the finest of cloths— and the saffron robe that is the antidote to the impurities of the afflictions.
Having offered beautiful garlands fashioned from clusters of excellent, tawny, and variegated flowers, along with robes of blue, yellow, white, red, and other lovely, radiant garments, he—
handsome and charming— bestowed divine, exquisite cloth upon the assembly of the sons of the Sugata.
Adorned with the garment of modesty, he becomes one of sharp intellect and a sovereign over all phenomena.
Thus ends the discourse on clothing.

XV. Those who constantly offer worship to the Saṅgha with beautiful flowers become like Śakra, endowed with supreme enjoyments, possessing bodies as radiant as the lotus and the moon, and graced with excellent fame; having swiftly conquered their enemies, they remain ever victorious. (SRKK 81)

Those who have offered sublime incense of noble fragrance to the Jina become human beings who wander upon the earth like jewels; their bodily scent is equal to a cluster of blue lotuses, and they possess pure, long, and beautiful eyes, with fame renowned for its stainlessness. SRKK 82.
With their limbs adorned with beryl, pearls, and jewels, and their entire bodies covered in silken garments,
these best of men are attended by all people as a result of offering fragrant substances to the Buddha.
Those who, freed from diseases and other causes of intense suffering, possess gentle countenances and a lovely complexion like gold,
and obtain a kingdom free from thorns— it is said that they do so by means of the practice of giving medicine to the Saṅgha.
Thus ends the discourse on flowers and so forth.

XVI. Regarding the Discourse on Prostration: When a universal monarch is repeatedly honored with devotion by the foremost of kings—whose cheeks are made beautiful by earrings—with palms joined and their own heads bowed, those who know the truth declare that this is due to his prostration before the Buddha.
Those who, as soon as they are born, attain lordship, whose birth is always in an eminent family,
and who travel about on elephants, horses, and vehicles— having first offered salutations to those even more excellent than themselves.
It spreads fame, bestows excellence, increases splendor,
removes all misfortune, and indeed wards off every enemy;
it ensures that the lineage of men in this world is destined for a happy rebirth.
And the salutation to the Lord of Sages inevitably bears fruit for one's ultimate welfare at the end.
That a king becomes a universal monarch (cakravartin), endowed with power and fame, his body adorned with the thirty-two marks,
and preeminent among rulers— this indeed is said to be the fruit of bowing to the Buddha.
Thus, considering the body to possess many virtues yet also to be fragile,
what wise person would perform any other physical action than bowing to the Buddha?
Who, seeing him from afar and fearing rebirth, would not pay him homage? By means of performing even a single prostration for his sake, one reaches the further shore of existence.
Thus concludes the discourse on prostration.

XVII. The Story of the Bestowing of Embers: In winter, within the inner chambers of their homes, those who are embraced by the pair of arms of their beloved women—wearing soft, large, and praiseworthy garments made from various kinds of fine wool—[do not perceive the cold].
That which lords of the earth, being prosperous, enjoy through various excellent flavors of food and drink—
that shall be the exceedingly sweet fruit of [an offering] dedicated to the community of monks at Ujjvālikā.

Having offered to the most excellent of the best sages a blazing torch— one enveloped by a fire expanding with waves of flames, possessing a terrifying sound, and destroying cold even in the winter season— one becomes possessed of radiant splendor in the worlds of gods and men.
Accompanied by Gandharvas, Asuras, and Kinnaras, with radiant countenances resembling the autumnal moon with its lightning-like flames,
those gods wander through heaven with glowing bodies, sporting and embraced by their beloveds.
Having given that with faith to the assembly of noble ones during the cold season, along with a bright lamp.
Those who, having conquered enemies mounted on elephants and horses, rule the earth in every direction,
with radiant faces and limbs adorned with gold— their reward is indeed the flame of Ujjvalikā.
Thus ends the story of the offering of the glowing coal.
XVIII. The Story of the Lamp: Even an object that is obstructed by mountains, situated in an extremely distant land, exceedingly minute, and shrouded by masses of intense darkness;
That which the monk Aniruddha beheld with his vision, situated as if upon the tip of a finger, was the fruit of the Sugata’s awakening by means of a lamp.
The Sugata indeed prophesied the state of Buddhahood for the woman who hung by the city wall by means of a lamp.
Who would not offer a garland of lamps to the Blessed One for the sake of attaining the eyes of the stainless Lord of Sages?
The sages have declared that the fruit of this garland of lamps for the Victor is that those people who see what is distant, subtle, concealed, or otherwise visible [attain such vision].
That kings are seen with bodies like the moon and eyes like long blue lotuses;
that gods, resembling excellent gold, illuminate the world of the gods with their own radiance;
and that a universal monarch (cakravartin) proceeds while illuminating the earth with hundreds of rays from his jewels.
All that comes to those who bear bodies through their devotion to the Lion of the Śākyas by means of offering lamps.
Whatever mortals shine in the world—those with eyes like blue lotuses, beautiful brows, and golden complexions;
and how Śakra, the king of gods, shines seated upon his celestial throne with his thousand eyes;
and how Brahmā, free from desire and honored by the foremost of the immortals, shines in his divine mansion—[all this is due to the power of the Tathāgata].
Having offered that garland of lamps at a shrine of the Teacher, men obtain a most excellent fruit.
Thus ends the story of the lamp.

XIX. Discourse on Monasteries: By the gift of monasteries for the community of noble mendicants from the four directions, kings delight upon the surfaces of excellent palaces charming in all seasons, accompanied by the songs of celestial nymphs and the voices of victorious life-sustaining melodies, together with the women of their harem, due to the absence of cold.
Having fully reported even the words of the Sage’s exhortation for the sake of the monastery of the community of noble monks and renunciants,
there shall be an immeasurable increase in merit arising from above, whether one is awake, moving, sleeping, or standing.
By the grace of him who has utterly shattered the mountain of the Kali age with the blow of the vajra of wisdom,
whoever constructs a monastery— endowed with all necessary requisites— for the sake of the Saṅgha,
shall [dwell] with beloved women upon the pillars and walls made of excellent jewels in the Vaijayanta palace.
He himself shall enjoy for a long time the celestial realm, which is delightful in all its seasons.

Having given to the preeminent and virtuous Gaṇa a principal house adorned with a splendid canopy, variegated lotuses, and beautiful cloths, its walls covered with blue and other colors, one attains Vaijayanta, the jewel of Indra’s palaces.
Thus concludes the discourse on the monastic dwellings.
XX. Discourse on the Gift of Beds and Seats:

Those kings by whom beds and seats were given to the One Supreme who has stilled the multitude of faults sleep at night upon couches spread with woolen rugs and stuffed with cotton, their limbs pressed by the thick breasts of beautiful women. (SRKK 104)

There, in the city of the immortals, he lies for a long time without fear upon a vast bed made of jewels, covered with variegated cloths, filled with the sweet warbling of celestial women, and suffused with the fragrance of fragrant perfumes; there he rests, with the arms of his beloved as his pillow.
This fruit which has been described as resulting from the gift of beds and seats to the community of monks.

With their bodies anointed with camphor, sandalwood, and excellent agallochum, their bodies resting between the breasts of divine women, they sleep eternally upon fine garments and excellent mattresses; this is due to their gift of beds and seats here to the stupa.
Thus concludes the discourse on the gift of beds and seats.
XXI. Discourse on the Realm:
Having swiftly conquered the four continents, Māndhātṛ went to the city of Maghavat; and from the Lord of the Thirty-three, he joyfully received half of his throne.
And for seven days, an incomparable rain of gold fell upon his palace; this was the wondrous fruit of the great gift bestowed upon worthy recipients.
And that vessel is fourfold, according to the distinctions of the suffering of the realms of rebirth and so forth;
therefore, a distinct and superior fruit arises for human beings from each of them.
Mortals with round faces, possessing a complexion like the blue water-lily or the moon, always having pure vision and broad chests,
obtain through their acts of giving delightful vehicles, beds, seats, and food among those in the human realm.
Those best of men who, filled with compassion, bestow gifts upon the sick, the wretched, and those of meager means—
having indeed attained prosperity, they become equal to kings and sport forever joyful with their sons and servants.

Men with moon-like faces, broad and excellent bodies, large eyes, and physiques resembling the morning sun—endowed with auspicious fame—obtain a kingdom free from the fear of enemies; for all this indeed comes from giving to one's own teachers and kinsmen.
That which kings travel upon, being honored by throngs of people with horses, chariots, and elephants, while golden-handled umbrellas resembling moonbeams block the piercing rays of the sun;
and that upon which a universal monarch, the supreme king of kings, travels across the earth together with hundreds of other noble rulers.
In a field that has been properly purified, this very fruit of excellent qualities arises from the seed of giving.
Māndhātā became a lord of the earth by giving mung beans; King Aśoka [became so] by giving dust; indeed, the one named Kapphiṇa became the lord of the thirty-three gods by giving five kinds of fruit;
and Citra, having given milk mixed with honey and jackfruit to one whose defilements were exhausted, [attained sovereignty].
Indeed, the status of a lord of the earth was attained, as was sovereignty in the abode of the Lord of the Gods, under the name Siṃha.
Even a great deal given is not at all fruitful when wealth is bestowed upon one who lacks a worthy recipient, like seed sown in a field overgrown with *balbaja* grass and thorns;
but it is fruitful when given to a recipient free from the stains of passion, hatred, and ignorance, and adorned with virtues.
Even a very small gift becomes great, just like the seed of a banyan tree.
Thus ends the discourse on fields.
XXII. Vicitrakathā:

He who here constantly writes the jewel of the Dharma, hears it, and always reflects upon it, or even if he should merely show respect toward it, he will always obtain the recollection of his past lives.

That in the world of the gods there exist excellent wish-fulfilling trees which accomplish all aims and serve as the cause of happiness for the supreme deities— that is the vast fruit of the gift of a cow.
That which attains full nourishment within the womb by being raised with pure essences; that which one drinks as honey and ghee in childhood, and milk again at the proper time;
and that drink which, in youth, possesses the luster of the filaments of a blooming blue lotus.
And in old age, one obtains the desired excellent essence arising from that gift of a cow.
He who, indeed, with joy and devotion, duly offers a beautiful lion-throne to the assembly,
that donor obtains excellent lion-thrones and the indestructible vajra-seat, which is worshipped by gods, nāgas, and siddhas.
The milk that kings constantly consume from golden vessels, enriched with flavors and other qualities,
and the lotus-faced women who possess abundant fortune, they obtain through the gift of a queen.
By the gift of vehicles to those who are always afflicted and by carrying those who are very weak,
a man indeed honors his elders and thereby attains supernatural power.
Kings are constantly carried by various horses adorned with golden plumes;
yet through the gift of vehicles, mortals likewise travel to very distant lands by means of supernatural power.
Adorned with necklaces, half-necklaces, and bracelets, those of beautiful complexion sport among the gods;
for the virtuous declare that this occurs through the gift of non-attachment to the Lord of the Thirty-three.
The wise person always consoles those who are afraid by means of the expression of speech;
he is never overcome by any Māras, and he constantly hears sweet words.
Those who here honor the Dharmadhātu on earth with the words of the Jina, which shatter the enemies that are the afflictions,
experience all the pleasures of saṃsāra and attain the supreme sovereignty over the Dharma.
The virtuous provide shelter at all times to those oppressed by fatigue;
they go constantly to the celestial realm, ever joyful, and always rejoice together with Śakra.
Those humans who plant beautiful groves here, as well as trees and fragrant flowers,
go to heaven after passing away, endowed with the enjoyment of gardens, garlands, and other delights.
Those people who construct a bridge over uneven terrain or even in the midst of water always go to the supreme heaven, endowed with enjoyments, their bodies adorned with excellent gold.
By constructing beautiful step-wells and ponds, men attain heaven;
and even while remaining as human beings in this very world, they obtain delightful and bliss-bestowing kingdoms.
Those excellent men who cause wells, monasteries, and shelters for living beings to be built as a means of protection against wind and sun, become like gods and attain happiness.
Those who offer parasols to those suffering greatly from the heat of the sun’s rays become members of the Jitaśatru assembly, always endowed with supreme happiness.
Those who devotedly give variegated footstools and sandals to all sentient beings travel for a very long time upon the finest vehicles, being constantly reborn among gods and humans.
Those who praise the Supreme Victor by extolling his qualities and honor all their gurus through the act of prostrating with their bodies,
obtain from the family of the guru both a noble birth and the analytical knowledge of speech.
Those who offer worship to the supreme Sugatas with mṛdaṅgas, vīṇās, paṭahas, and other instruments,
when born as humans, possess most pleasing speech and hear sounds of most pleasing form.
If a person joyfully erects a staff, a parasol, or a bell at the stūpa of the Sugata,
or constructs a row of parasols, by that act he attains vast prosperity.
The virtuous declare that the gift of land bestows upon a man on earth sovereign power over all directions, endowed with strength and adorned with armlets and pearl ornaments.
Whoever fashions an excellent image of the Jina, or a stūpa endowed with the finest parasols,
and whoever enshrines a relic here in this world, that person attains heaven by means of that act.
Those who constantly perform great acts of plastering with clay and cow dung dedicated to the Buddha,
or who offer flowers, fruits, food, or drink, obtain royal power.
Those who offer to the Saṅgha magnificent lamps, various perfumes, flowers, incense, or molasses drinks, as well as gold, shall become endowed with celestial happiness.
Those people who here diligently cleanse the courtyard of a stūpa, the excellent reliquary, the monastery,
and remove the withered flower offerings from them, become golden-hued and beautiful to behold.
Those who bestow glowing embers upon the virtuous during the onset of cold, or provide clothing, or even a house, or various drinks, or an excellent maiden, become happy in their place of birth.

Indeed, that wise person who abstains from taking life shall live long on earth, freed from all diseases, and, ever joyful, shall attain incomparable and constant happiness; he truly enjoys the various pleasures born of the gods.
He who, upon seeing the wealth of another, does not commit theft and instead maintains watchfulness for the purpose of protection,
shall attain an immeasurable abundance of riches that cannot be taken away by hundreds of thieves, kings, or others.
He who here avoids the wife of another indeed obtains a wife of pleasing form;
for one born of an enemy is never at all trustworthy to people in this world.
Just as the fragrance of a blue lotus, being of a pleasing form, wafts forth constantly,
even so does the fragrance of a person waft from the mouth of one who speaks no untruth.
One who is forever free from slander attains alliance with true friends, honor from the king, a devoted wife, children, and servants, as well as noble enjoyments and immeasurable happiness.
The man who refrains from harsh speech hears sweet sounds of joy and always pleasant words; he is born among gods and mortals. (SRKK 146)
Indeed, whose speech is always devoted to dharma, artha, and truth becomes eternally most beloved here in this world;
such a person receives honor through many kinds of jewels, and upon passing away, shall go to the world of the gods for infinite happiness.
He indeed does not possess intense passion here, is constantly endowed with noble enjoyments,
possesses authoritative speech, and is possessed of great fame— he who is truly free from craving for the wealth of others.
Such a person constantly attains a pleasing appearance, abundant happiness, sovereignty, wealth, and so forth in this world;
by the power of a mind of loving-kindness, a human being rightly reaches the state of Brahmā here.
Those men who desire to fully attain heaven and liberation must always cultivate the view of existence;
for it is the supreme view, indeed the very root of all that is wholesome.
Merit that brings about the sublime happiness of the three worlds does not sprout in one whose mind is devoid of faith;
therefore, a wise person should always cultivate faith, which is the repository of all the jewels of virtue.
Faith is the mother of virtue, just as a biological mother is; therefore, it should be established first in the minds of virtuous people.
For one devoid of the instrument of faith is indeed incapable of grasping the heap of jewels that are the true dharmas conducive to enlightenment.
Just as one who has fallen from his position of authority does not obtain the fruits of sovereignty,
so too one who has fallen away from the faculty of faith does not obtain the fruits of the noble ones.
Therefore, a wise person should constantly direct a serene mind toward the Sugatas and those who act for the benefit of others;
for there is nothing else that pacifies all faults as faith does, which burns away the entire multitude of defects.
Miserable, poorly dressed, and deluded, with hands marked by begging bowls,
they indeed demonstrate to the world such a fruit for one who does not give.
With bodies like scorched pillars, these beggars wander from house to house like hungry ghosts, perpetually oppressed by hunger; raising their arms and crying "Give!",
they stand even while being driven away at a distance by packs of dogs.
Generally, these people have never given even a small amount of food to anyone, not even once.
With needle-like mouths, hollow eyes, and withered limbs, clad only in their hair, their radiance completely drained by the rays of the sun—
these hungry ghosts (pretas), who are perpetually tormented by a longing for water, proclaim that this is the fruit of one who was stingy in giving drink.
Generosity is all-encompassing happiness, the remover of great fear, fortune, and the bestower of great wealth; it is the ground of various forms of vast skillfulness, adorned with every virtue.
Therefore, generosity is the pacifier of manifold defects and the dispeller of the terrors of saṃsāra.
Men should diligently perform that which brings about auspiciousness and thoroughly dries up hunger, thirst, and other such afflictions.
Thus ends the "Diverse Narratives."
Summary Verses:
Encouraging merit, hearing [the teaching], which is difficult to obtain; the image, bathing, likewise perfume, the parasol, and the enshrinement of relics. (1)
The maṇḍala, food, drink, clothing, and the description of flowers and so forth; prostration, incense, lamps, the monastery, and the bed and seat. // 2 //
"The Field," "The Variegated," and "The End"—these twenty-two discourses have been proclaimed extensively in various ways for the further description of giving. (3)
XXIII. Discourse on Morality:

Just as a pond filled with water but containing snakes, or a tree with blossoming branches yet covered in thorns, so too is a person who, though endowed with learning, wealth, and noble birth, is averse to morality. (SRKK 159)
Better it would be to be poor yet possessed of good character than to be wealthy yet unadorned with virtues;
for even in a state of poverty, a virtuous person is praised, and the essence of virtues excels even nectar.
The wise honor one who possesses virtue, even if they are powerful, wealthy, or high-minded.
Therefore, let that man who desires honor even from the presence of a king protect his own moral conduct alone.
In this world, the pleasure born of sense objects is accompanied by fear and enmity; however, for one whose self is fixed on the Dharma and whose mind is disciplined, there is supreme happiness.
Therefore, a person who desires to attain noble, unshakable, and sublime happiness should protect their ethical conduct alone.
The terror that enters one whose morality and discipline have fallen away at the time of destruction does not exist for the virtuous person.
Therefore, he who desires to go to the next world at the end with a joyful discipline should guard his morality alone.
Through morality that is firm in its resolve, one goes to heaven—not through self-exhaustion nor by the wrong paths created by false views.
Therefore, even without dwelling in the forest and even without the [ascetic] insignia, he who desires heaven should guard his morality alone.
Ethical discipline is protection against destruction, theft, and obscuration; ethical discipline is the supreme wealth of the noble ones, which cannot be stolen by others.
Ethical discipline is a steadfast friend that follows one even in the state of total peace; ethical discipline is an ornament even without physical ornaments.
Indeed, there is no beneficial friend equal to ethical discipline, nor is there a relative with such affectionate intent as ethical discipline;
for what mother or father would wish to provide for their child anything other than ethical discipline, which bestows powerful fruit and brings true welfare?
Thus concludes the discourse on ethical discipline.
XXIV. Discourse on Forbearance:
All this well-performed conduct—generosity and the worship of the Sugatas—which has been practiced throughout thousands of eons, anger destroys it all. (SRKK 167)
There is no evil equal to hatred, and no austerity equal to patience;
therefore, one should cultivate patience with effort through various methods.
When the thorn of hatred remains in the heart, the mind finds no peace, it does not enjoy joy or happiness, and it attains neither sleep nor steadfastness.
Those who harbor hatred do not come to an end even if one were to kill them throughout one's entire life;
however, he who destroys anger alone has thereby destroyed all his enemies.
Blazing with the fuel of conceptual construction, the living being first burns himself with the fire of anger; he may or may not burn others later.
Old age for those possessed of beauty, anger even for those with sight, and the destruction of virtue, wealth, and pleasure— therefore, one should restrain anger.
For these have been impelled by my own karma and have become doers of harm toward me;
since they will go to the hells, have they not indeed already been slain by me?
Relying upon these, my great evil is destroyed through my forbearance;
yet, by relying upon me, they go to hells of long-lasting suffering.
"I alone am the one who does them harm, and they are my benefactors;
why, O base-minded one, do you become angry by reversing this fact?"

If you are angry with the instigator, setting aside the primary agent such as the wielder of the staff, then that [instigator] too is impelled by hatred; let my hatred instead be directed toward that hatred.
Thus concludes the discourse on patience.
XXV. Discourse on Vigor.
For vigor is the storehouse of all jewels of virtue; by the great raft of vigor, one crosses over all calamities.
When one has mounted the chariot of vigor, there is no object in this world that, upon reflection, cannot be attained. (SRKK 177)

That which consists in slaying enemies and attaining unsurpassed victory in battles crowded with elephants, horses, and infantry, and teeming with iron arrows, javelins, and battle-axes— that is the manifest prowess of a great warrior in this world.

Having crossed, by their valor alone, the oceans— terrifying with the breaking of towering waves violently tossed by swarms of sea-monsters— as easily as a mere puddle in a cow’s footprint, heroes acquire wealth in the form of jewels of priceless virtue.
Endowed with the power to counteract passions such as attachment— which are like fierce-bodied serpents—
and correctly inspiring others to adopt the virtue that purifies the minds of the noble,
these mortals, full of vigor, dwell upon the most beautiful slopes of Mount Meru.
They rejoice for a long time, embraced by the noose-like vine-arms of the beautiful celestial maidens.
That the gods who dwell in celestial palaces in the sky experience a state of well-being free from the pairs of opposites—
that is the splendor resulting from diligence that has been firmly established for the sake of producing exceedingly vast fruits.
Thus concludes the discourse on diligence.
XXVI.
Having overcome the host of enemies that are the afflictions, the steadfast attain the state of the glory of perfect enlightenment;
they bestow the gift of the factors of awakening upon the virtuous, for they proclaim meditation to be the cause therein.
Having torn asunder all the accumulations of defects such as passion, which serve as the sole cause for the continuity of birth,
those men whose minds are like space and for whom a clod of earth and gold are equal become, through meditation, the very causes of virtuous qualities.

Having conquered the host of enemies that are the afflictions, having achieved their goal in every way through the crushing of the forces of evil, and having attained the glory of perfect enlightenment— which consists of supreme qualities and is difficult for others to obtain— those Lords of Men, free from the fear of enemies, exercise sovereignty over sentient beings through their wisdom.
The Noble Ones have declared that meditation therein is the sole cause for the multitude of virtues, a treasury of all qualities.

Having forever rent asunder the darkness of delusion, the Sun of the Perfectly Awakened One brings forth the illumination of wisdom everywhere; he is the cause for gods and humans—this is the preeminent samādhi therein.
Thus concludes the discourse on meditative concentration.
XXVII. Discourse on Wisdom:
The form of a man devoid of the wealth of wisdom is like a painted image, lacking substance within.
For one endowed with intelligence, the desired fruit arises through vigor; yet vigor devoid of intelligence is an enemy that leads to one's own destruction.

Even a person who possesses knowledge of the middle and the end can discern their own births—past and future, separated by many lifetimes—along with their family names, lineages, and clans; those who know this declare that to be the power of wisdom.
In the world of mortals, the Buddha shatters the great mass of defilements and darkness,
creates the light of wisdom, and constantly strikes down the multitude of faults in men;
he is the instructor of the sense faculties and knows the minds of all other beings in every possible way.
In that regard as well, they proclaim wisdom to be the constant cause, the mother of auspicious and excellent qualities.
Even when deeply submerged in an ocean of tasks in the midst of battle, preeminent men obtain victory through the power of wisdom; for that wisdom is the cause of auspiciousness.
Therefore, let wisdom alone, which accomplishes the purpose of all virtues, be cultivated;

for men devoid of wisdom do not shine, like lamps at dawn. Having realized this, one should apply oneself to the practice of what is beneficial for oneself and others, and to the accomplishment of the True Dharma.
Having conquered the hosts of afflictions, may those who seek the Dharma and delight in the welfare of others sport in the virtuous goal. // 190 //
Thus concludes the discourse on wisdom.
These six perfections alone are the repositories of the jewels of the qualities of heaven and liberation for men on this earth;
knowing this, what man devoted to accomplishing his own welfare would not constantly exert firm effort toward them? (SRKK 191)
Thus ends the discourse on the perfections in the *Subhāṣitaratnakaraṇḍaka*.
The work of the teacher Śūra.
